newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia manufacturing exports to rebound.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia manufacturing exports to rebound.

text.p: Malaysia's exports of manufactured goods are expected to recover slightly in 1997 after growth slowed last year due to weak electronics demand, International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz said on Thursday.
"We expect some uptake this year," she said when asked about the electronics sector at a briefing on manufacturing in 1996.
"Companies in the electronics sector continue to expand their infrastructure" to prepare for an expected rebound this year, Rafidah said. She did not give any projections.
The electrical, electronics and machinery industry grew 9.9 percent in the first 10 months of last year, much slower than the 20.9 percent in the same period a year earlier.
However the industry remained the leading manufacturing sub-sector and contributed about 48 percent of manufacturing output.

Economists said the global electronics outlook should show some improvement in the latter part of the year. "It's kind of bottomed out. Hopefully, things will get better by the second half," said Nik Ahmad Fauzan, economist at investment house Vickers Ballas.
Rafidah said the broader manufacturing sector was expected to grow by 12.5 percent this year, lower than the 12.8 percent in 1996 and against 14.5 percent in 1995.

"The moderation in manufacturing output in 1996 was due to deceleration in the growth of some export-oriented industries, particularly electronics, due to a softening of external demand," Rafidah said. Malaysia's manufactured exports grew by 5.8 percent against 22.9 percent in 1995.
The Malaysian economy expanded by 8.2 percent last year for its ninth straight year of at least eight percent growth.
Gross Domestic Product grew by 9.5 percent in 1996 and the government has forecast 8.0 percent growth this year.
Economists said the steady expansion of the manufacturing sector this year was not unwelcome after fears last year that the economy was growing too fast.

"The fundamentals look good but we'll probably slow down further on the effects of high interest rates and export slowdown. This should be welcomed to take some pressure off rates," said Credit Lyonnais economist Chan Kok Peng.

Rafidah said proposed manufacturing capital investments totalled 41.7 billion ringgit ($16.8 billion) last year, a 55.3 percent rise over 1995's 26.9 billion. Of this, 17.6 billion ringgit, or 42.2 percent, were from foreign investors.
Manufacturing contributed 34.5 percent to the country's GDP in 1996 against 33.1 percent the previous year, the minister said.
